objective: understand the commutative law of addition and form a family of addition and subtraction facts.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Use it to stimulate discussions relating to commutative law. Ask students to find the total number of poi for 11 red poi and 5 black poi and to write an equation for the solution (11 + 5 = 16). Ask them whether the solution would be the same if there were 5 black poi and 11 red poi. Would the equation be the same? (5 + 11 = 16) Guide students to see that both equations will give us the same answer. Try this with other sets of 2 numbers (e.g. 8 black poi and 7 red poi), and then 3 numbers (e.g. 4 red poi, 5 black poi and 6 blue poi). Help students conclude that when we add, the order of the numbers does not affect the answer.
Then ask students, now that we know the total, what can we do to find the number of black poi? Will the equation be the same? Can we use the same numbers to make a subtraction equation? (16 – 5 = 11) What if we want to find the number of red poi? What does the equation look like? (16 – 11 = 5) Guide them to see that with the same 3 numbers, we can form a family of addition and subtraction facts.
During Guided Practice, students are completing families of addition and subtraction facts.
formative_assessment:
find the addition facts for any 2 numbers.
Students can find the subtraction facts for any 2 numbers.
Students can find the complete family of addition and subtraction facts for any 2 numbers.

Can students make the link between the Base 10 materials and the column addition? Allow time for students to understand what each digit represents in the column method using both Base 10 materials and the number bond representation.

objective: add two 3-digit numbers without renaming, using the column method of addition.
approach:
Students learnt the column method of addition in Year 3. In this lesson, help them to apply this knowledge to adding 3-digit numbers. Use this lesson to make sure any misconceptions are eradicated, especially for struggling learners.
To begin this lesson, show the class the Explore task. Ask some students to demonstrate how the number 413 could be shown in terms of hundreds, tens and ones using Base 10 materials. Do the same for 582. Ask the class where we should begin when we want to add 582 to 413. Get them to add the ones, tens and then hundreds. Ask students if they can represent this addition using the column method. Give them time to write the column method and help struggling students to recall how to do this. Then ask students to explain why the addition always starts from adding the ones. Guide them to relate addition to the renaming from ones to tens to hundreds.
During Master, emphasise the importance of placing digits with the same place value together when adding using the column method. Use Base 10 materials alongside the column method to better illustrate this.
During Guided Practice, the emphasis is on the column method.

objective: add a 3-digit number to ones with renaming.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and ask them to discuss with their partners how they could add 7 to 345. Allow them to use Base 10 materials to get to the answer. Then ask them to share their answers and gather their methods. Show the class all the methods as illustrated in the textbook.
Method 1 is a bridging process using the expanded column method. It helps students to see the renaming process and understand that the column method essentially adds by renaming. This can be used for struggling learners who are not yet ready to move to the standard column method.
Method 2 is the standard column method. Use Base 10 materials as well as number bonds alongside the column method to make the method explicit. Compare the similarities between methods 1 and 2 so students can see the link between them.
Method 3 uses knowledge of number bonds to make the next ten, and then add the remainder of the ones. It is important to go through all the three methods so that students gain an understanding of the question and numbers, rather than just following a procedure.
During Guided Practice, provide students with digit cards to form the addition statements.

count on to add a 3-digit number to ones with renaming.

objective: add a 3-digit number to multiples of 10 with renaming.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask the students what they think will change when the numbers are added to each score. What do they notice about the tens place? Discuss the methods from previous lessons that could be used to find a solution to the problem. Agree that the addition statements are 593 + 50, 695 + 70 and 498 + 50.
Show Lulu's addition statement: 593 + 50. Ask students, when using Base 10 materials and a place-value chart, what happens to the tens when there are more than 9 tens. Along with the Base 10 materials, show the expanded column method and help students link the column method to the concrete representation. Repeat this using Tama's example: 695 + 70.
After going through these two examples (593 + 50 and 695 + 70), ask students to add the same numbers using the standard column method. Then ask them to add 498 and 50 using a number bond.
After practising addition using all the three methods, ask students to compare the 3 numbers – 593, 695 and 498. Guide them to use approximation: 593 is about 600, 695 is about 700 and 498 is about 500; then compare 600, 700 and 500. It will be much easier to see which number is greatest or smallest using this method. Help them to see that a 3-digit number with 9 tens is very close to the next hundred. Students can check the calculations using a calculator to evaluate their approximations.
During Guided Practice, students are performing a similar task to the Explore activity, with specific criteria around how to use the numbers.

count on to add a 3-digit number to a multiple of 10 with renaming.
Students can use Base 10 materials to add a 3-digit number to a multiple of 10 with renaming.

approach:

objective: subtract from a 3-digit number with the renaming of 1 ten into 10 ones.
approach:

Ask students if they notice that the 3-digit number is placed above the 2-digit number and if they know why. Guide them to relate it to the subtraction equation, 652 – 25; the column method is essentially another way to present the subtraction equation. Ask students why 25 is aligned to the right and not to the left. Guide them to recall that the ones must be placed in the ones column and the tens must be placed in the tens column.
Provide students with Base 10 materials and ask them to represent 652 using the materials. Ask them to show how the 5 ones can be subtracted. Lead students to rename 1 ten into 10 ones. Show the process of renaming using the column method so that students can relate the 'crossing out' to renaming. It is important here that students understand why they are crossing out the tens column and ones column and changing the numbers. Then proceed to subtract the ones, tens and hundreds.
During Guided Practice, students are practising using Base 10 materials to show when they need to rename and when they do not.

objective: subtract from a multiple of 100 with renaming.
approach:
In this lesson, students learn to rename twice before doing the subtraction. It involves renaming the hundreds and then the tens before subtracting the ones. In these questions, students generally tend to lose perspective of the numbers used and focus instead on the procedure, therefore often making mistakes resulting in an unusual answer. It is important to remind students how a number is composed and allow them time to estimate so they can check their answer is close to their estimate.
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task and give them enough time to solve this problem by themselves in groups.
Allow them to use Base 10 materials to represent 400. Then get them to start by subtracting the ones. They will need to rename 1 ten as there is 0 ones in 400. However, there are also 0 tens in 400, therefore they have to rename 1 hundred into 10 tens. Once there are 10 tens, students can rename 1 ten into 10 ones. Then they can proceed to subtract.
After they have the answer 236, ask them to use the column method to subtract. Did they get the same answer? If not, where did they go wrong? Ask them to check through the renaming done on the column method to check they have done it correctly.
During Guided Practice, encourage students to use the column method and show the renaming.

objective: solve word problems using addition and subtraction.
approach:
This is the first of four lessons on the bar model. Students have come across bar modelling in Year 2 and we will now build on their experience and competence.
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them how they might come to the correct answer using cubes. Ask if the process can be represented using the squares in their exercise books/journals. Could 4 cubes be 4 squares and 3 cubes which represented 3 cupcakes be represented on paper with 3 squares?
Refer to Master 1 to explain that we do not always have to use one square to represent each unit. Show students that we can have a bar to represent 4 cupcakes and another bar to represent 3 cupcakes. Ask them how long the second bar should be if we are going to represent it as 3 cupcakes. Students should realise that the second bar should be shorter than the first as it represents fewer cupcakes. Help them recall that when we want to find the total, we can add the two parts, which are 4 and 3.
Refer to Master 2 to show students 17 + 21. Guide them to see that it is similar to Master 1, except for the numbers involved. Ask them to try drawing a bar model to represent the problem. They can use the previous bar model as a reference. Once they have drawn a bar model, help them to label it and then proceed to find the number of cupcakes they have altogether
During Guided Practice, students are solving problems with the help of bar models.

use concrete materials to represent items in a problem.
Students can draw a bar model to represent a number of items in a problem
Students can label all parts of the bar model with numbers and words.
Students can determine what information is missing from a bar model.
Students can apply addition and subtraction strategies from the chapter to bar model scenarios.

approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. Ask them if they know how many more apples than oranges there are. To do that, students must know how many apples are on the first tree and how many oranges are on the second tree. Draw a bar to represent the apples, then draw another bar below it to represent the oranges and label the two bars. Help students to see where 'more pieces of fruit' are represented on the bar model, then label that part of the bar model. Guide them to see that they can use subtraction to find the answer, since we know both the number of apples and oranges.
Show the class Master 2 and discuss the problem with them. Lead them to see that this problem is similar to the previous one, except the numbers used are different. Ask them to try drawing the bar model for this problem, then model the drawing for them on the board. Guide students to draw the first bar for Charles, then another bar below it for Meilani. Ask them if Meilani's bar should be longer or shorter based on the information from the problem. Then lead students to label the bar model with the information given. Since we know the number of chocolates Charles and Meilani each have, we can find out how many more by subtraction.
During Guided Practice, students are practising drawing comparison models to represent the problems.

objective: solve 'more than' and 'fewer than' word problems using addition and subtraction.
approach:
To begin this lesson, show students the Explore task. What is the question asking us to find? How can they draw a bar model to represent the information from the question? Would it be better to use a part–whole or comparison model? Why? Give students enough time to work on this together. After some discussion, ask a student to draw the bars for Basket A and Basket B. Then ask students to fill in as much information on their model as possible.
Try to guide students if they have missed anything that has been given in the question. Highlight the excess part of Basket A (compared to Basket B) on the bar model. Ask the class how they can work out this part of the bar. If needed, remind them about the previous lesson, which looked at the number of apples and oranges. Ask students what calculation is needed to find out the excess in the bar representing Basket A. Ask them what this section gives us. Make sure everyone is aware that it gives us how many more tennis balls Basket A has, but also how many fewer tennis balls Box B has.
During Guided Practice, students are solving more word problems using comparison bar models.
